data.heading: What Is 3D Visualization?
data.body:
Most interior disputes come from a gap between what a client imagined and what was drawn. Visualisation closes that gap. You see the finished ceiling, the veneer direction, the lighting temperature and the furniture layout while everything is still editable.

Because our render team sits beside our design and site teams, what you approve is what we build — no reinterpretation between image and installation.

items.question: How fast can I get a render?
items.answer: Basic interior and exterior renders are typically delivered in 2 to 5 days. We confirm the delivery date before work begins.

items.question: What files do I receive?
items.answer: Renders arrive as high resolution PNG and JPG files, with 4K and print quality available. Animations arrive as MOV and MP4 files.

items.question: How many revisions are included?
items.answer: Every brief includes two revision rounds. Extra rounds and finish options can be added if needed.

items.question: Can I commission renders without using Woodex to build?
items.answer: Yes. Woodex 3D Studio is a standalone service. Architects, interior designers and developers commission visualization from us even when another practice is executing the build.

items.question: Do you do exterior renders and animations?
items.answer: Yes. Photorealistic exterior renders and walkthrough/flyover animations are part of the studio's core scope.

items.question: What is a sciography study?
items.answer: A sciography study shows the sun path and shadow patterns across a site and building. It helps with planning, daylight analysis and environmental review.

items.question: Do you produce 360° virtual tours?
items.answer: Yes. We produce interactive 360° tours for early sales and marketing, so viewers can explore the space online from any device.

items.question: What information do you need to start?
items.answer: Drawings or concept references, the camera angles you need and your deadline. From that, we confirm scope, turnaround and quote within one business day.

data.heading: Architecture vs Interior Design vs Fit-Out

items.question: What is the difference between an architect and a civil engineer?
items.answer: An architect designs the building: its layout, form, elevations and spatial experience. A civil or structural engineer designs the beams, columns and foundations. Woodex handles the architecture and coordinates the structural team.

items.question: Do I need PCATP registration for my house design?
items.answer: Requirements vary by project and authority. PCATP registration may be needed for some commercial, multi-unit or formal submissions. Woodex has PCATP-certified architects and can advise on your project.

items.question: How long does a house design take?
items.answer: A typical 5–10 Marla house takes about 4–6 weeks, while a 1–2 Kanal house may take 6–10 weeks. Authority processing is separate.

items.question: What is included in the architecture fee?
items.answer: The standard scope includes concept plans, 3D views, design development, working drawings and submission preparation. Structural coordination is included for full-package projects. Government fees are separate.

items.question: Can I get only a front elevation designed?
items.answer: Yes. The standalone elevation service includes a photorealistic 3D facade view and a 2D elevation drawing for your contractor.

items.question: Do you work on projects outside Lahore?
items.answer: Yes. Site visits outside Lahore are arranged separately, and much of the review process can be handled through virtual meetings and digital drawings.

items.question: Can Woodex handle architecture, interiors, fit-out and furniture?
items.answer: Yes. These can be commissioned as coordinated services, giving you one team from building design through the finished interior.

items.question: Can I make changes after design approval?
items.answer: Yes, but late changes can affect drawings, coordination, approvals, cost and timing. We review the impact with you before revising the approved package.

data.heading: Layout and storage
data.body:
Keep the wet zone (shower) apart from the dry zone (vanity and WC) with a glass screen and a level threshold. Place the WC away from the door line and give the vanity a deep drawer rather than open shelves. In compact bathrooms, a niche in the shower wall replaces bulky caddies.

Lighting matters more than it seems: a soft ceiling light, a mirror light at face height and a low night light make the room usable at any hour.

Plan sockets carefully: a shaver point at the mirror, a protected circuit for the geyser, and nothing within reach of the shower.

data.heading: Survey first
data.body:
Every renovation starts with a proper survey. Structure, plumbing, electrical load and damp are checked before the design is drawn.

Surprises found on paper cost a conversation. Surprises found mid-build cost money and weeks.

data.heading: Freeze scope, hold a buffer
data.body:
Decide the full scope and freeze it before work begins. Changes mid-build are the main reason renovations overrun.

Hold a buffer of 10 to 15 percent of the budget for what the walls reveal. If you do not spend it, it is yours.

data.heading: Sequence the trades
data.body:
Renovations run in a fixed order: demolition and civil work, plumbing and electrical, then joinery, paint and finishing. Each trade needs the one before it finished.

Rushing the sequence creates rework. A realistic programme agreed upfront keeps everyone honest.

data.heading: Living through it
data.body:
Decide early whether you stay or move out. Living through a renovation saves rent but slows work and tests patience.

If you stay, agree on dust control, working hours and which rooms stay usable. Put it in writing. See our residential renovation service for how we manage occupied homes.

Before the last payment, walk through every room with a written list. Check finishes in daylight, test every switch and tap, open every door and drawer, and look for leaks under sinks.

data.heading: Why one per-sq-ft number never tells the full story
data.body:
Owners usually ask for a single figure: what is the house renovation cost in Lahore per square foot? It is a fair question, but the honest answer is that the rate depends on what sits behind the walls as much as what goes on them. A cosmetic refresh and a full services upgrade can share the same floor area and still be priced worlds apart.

So before comparing quotes, agree on what kind of renovation you are actually buying. The tier decides the rate far more than the size of the house.

rows.label: Refresh
rows.value: Paint, lighting swaps, minor carpentry, fixture changes Â· Lowest

rows.label: Upgrade
rows.value: New flooring, kitchen and bath refits, false ceilings, partial rewiring Â· Medium

rows.label: Full renovation
rows.value: Layout changes, complete plumbing and electrical, new finishes throughout Â· Highest

data.heading: What moves the rate up or down
data.body: Each of these can shift the per-sq-ft rate more than the brand of paint you choose.

facts.value: Condition of services. Old wiring or galvanised pipes found after demolition are the most common budget shock.
Layout changes. Moving a kitchen or bathroom means new drainage falls, not just new tiles.
Finish level. Imported porcelain, solid wood and stone sit in a different bracket to local equivalents.
Joinery volume. Wardrobes, kitchens and wall panelling add up quickly.

data.heading: Costs owners forget to budget
data.body:
Plan a contingency from day one. In our experience the items that catch Lahore owners off guard are rarely the big ones:

A good quotation names these lines even when the amount is provisional. If they are missing, ask.

facts.value: Debris removal and site cleaning
Waterproofing under new bathrooms and on roofs
Upgraded electrical load and a new distribution board
Temporary accommodation or storage

data.heading: How to get a quotation you can trust
data.body:
For a first rough range, our cost estimator gives a starting point in a few minutes. For a firm number, a site visit is the only honest route. You can also see what a complete scope looks like on our complete home redesign page.

Share your floor plan and brief and the Woodex team will come back with the right next step.

facts.value: Start with a site survey and measured drawings, not a phone estimate.
Freeze the scope room by room before pricing.
Ask for an itemised bill of quantities with material specifications.
Compare quotes line by line, never just the total.
Tier beats size: refresh, upgrade and full renovation are priced on different logic.
Hidden services cost the most: wiring, plumbing and waterproofing drive surprises.
Itemise everything: a bill of quantities is the only fair way to compare quotes.

items.question: What is the average house renovation cost in Lahore per square foot?
items.answer: There is no reliable single average because the scope changes the rate so much. A paint-and-fixtures refresh and a full rewire with new layouts can differ several times over for the same area. Decide the tier, list the items and price those.

items.question: Is it cheaper to renovate or rebuild in Lahore?
items.answer: Renovation is usually more economical when the structure is sound and the layout mostly works. If foundations, roof slabs or the plan itself are failing, rebuilding can be better value. A structural check settles it.

items.question: How much contingency should I keep for a renovation?
items.answer: Keep a clear contingency line separate from the main budget, larger for older houses where services are unknown. Use it only for genuine discoveries, not for upgrades chosen mid-way.

items.question: Can I renovate one floor at a time?
items.answer: Yes. Phasing floor by floor works well if services are planned for the whole house first, so you do not open finished rooms again later.

items.question: How long does a full house renovation take in Lahore?
items.answer: It depends on the scope and how quickly decisions are made. Once the scope is fixed, a phase-by-phase plan gives a reliable schedule.

On many projects, the best result comes from a designer and a contractor working together. The designer defines what is built and checks quality; the contractor manages labour and delivery.

Agree who is responsible for what in writing: drawings, purchasing, site supervision, quality checks and snagging. Clear roles prevent the most common disputes.

data.heading: Next steps
data.body:
If you are planning a renovation or new interior, start by writing down what you want to change, what must stay and the date you need the space ready. Take photos of the space as it is today and collect a few images of interiors you like.

Decide how involved you want to be. If you have little time for site visits and supplier meetings, one coordinated team is usually the calmer option.

When you are ready, see our services page or book a site visit or studio meeting. A designer can review your space, talk through options and prepare a written, itemised quote.

data.heading: The third route: design-build
data.body:
Design-build keeps design and execution with one team, so the people who draw the details are answerable for building them. It suits owners who do not want to referee between two parties. Whichever route you choose, insist on drawings, an itemised quotation and one named person responsible on site.

See how this works on our renovation and fit-out pages, or talk to the studio.

Share your floor plan and brief and the Woodex team will come back with the right next step.

facts.value: Different jobs: designers plan and detail, contractors build.
The gap is the risk: someone must own drawing-to-site.
Design-build puts both under one accountable team.

items.question: Is it cheaper to hire a contractor instead of an interior designer?
items.answer: The upfront cost is lower, but rework from unclear details often wipes out the saving on anything beyond simple repairs.

items.question: Can an interior designer manage the contractor for me?
items.answer: Many do, through site supervision. Confirm the number of visits and who signs off work.

items.question: What is design-build?
items.answer: One team handles design and construction, so drawings and execution stay connected and responsibility is clear.

items.answer: Ask for past sites to visit, an itemised quotation, who supervises daily, and how changes are priced.

data.heading: Controls make layers useful
data.body:
Put each layer on its own switch or dimmer so you can set scenes: bright for cleaning, soft for evenings, focused for work. In larger homes and offices, simple scene controls add comfort without complexity. Plan switches with the furniture layout, not after it.

Lighting is usually planned together with the ceiling; see false ceiling design and cost.

data.heading: Colour temperature and colour rendering
data.body:
Colour temperature, measured in kelvin, describes how warm or cool light looks. Warm white (2700K to 3000K) suits living rooms and bedrooms. Neutral white (3500K to 4000K) suits kitchens, bathrooms and offices where you need to see clearly.

Colour rendering (CRI) describes how true colours look under the light. Choose CRI 90 or higher wherever skin tones, food or fabrics matter, such as dressing areas, kitchens and dining rooms.

data.heading: Switching and control
data.body:
Good lighting is as much about control as fittings. Put each layer on its own switch, so ambient, task and accent light can be used separately. Add dimmers in living and dining rooms.

Two-way switches at both ends of corridors and stairs, and bedside switches for the main light, are small details that make a home much easier to live in.

July and August bring heavy rain and high humidity. Damp rises through walls, timber swells and paint blisters where moisture is trapped.

Underspending tends to hit the things staff feel every day, such as acoustics, task lighting and enough power outlets. data.heading: Zoning: focus, meet, social

Every office needs three kinds of space. Focus zones for deep work, meeting zones for collaboration, and social zones where the team actually talks.

Getting the ratio right matters more than any single finish. Watch how your team works for a week before the plan is drawn.

Open offices fail on noise, not looks. Acoustic panels, soft flooring and proper ceiling treatment keep conversations from carrying across the floor.

Daylight belongs near desks. Meeting rooms and services can sit deeper in the plan, where borrowed light does the job.

data.body:
The office should feel like your company, not a catalogue. A restrained palette with one or two brand moments, done well, beats logos on every wall.

Reception carries the most weight. It is the first thing clients see and the last thing new hires remember from day one.

Leave enough space between desks for people to move and for privacy on calls. Cramped rows look efficient on paper but reduce comfort and concentration.

A restaurant has two parts: the dining space guests see, and the kitchen, storage and staff areas they do not. Both affect cost, and the back of house often needs more investment than owners expect.

data.heading: Service flow
data.body:
Staff routes decide everything. The path from kitchen to table should be short, straight and clear of guest circulation.

Map a full service in the plan: entry, seating, ordering, delivery, clearing and payment. Bottlenecks drawn on paper are cheap; bottlenecks built in tile are not.

data.heading: Seating mix
data.body:
Revenue lives in the seating mix. Twos that combine into fours, a few larger tables, and bar seating for solo diners and waiting parties.

Comfort sets dwell time. Fast casual wants turnover-friendly seating; fine dining earns it back in longer, higher value covers.

data.heading: Mood versus durability
data.body:
Mood brings guests in; durability keeps the business running. Choose materials that look rich and survive nightly cleaning: sealed timber, commercial upholstery, scrubbable paint.

Lighting does the heavy lifting for mood. Warm, dimmable layers flatter food and faces, while brighter task light keeps service areas safe.

data.heading: Kitchen adjacency
data.body:
The kitchen and dining room are one system. Pass, dish return and bar support should sit tight against the kitchen line to cut steps and noise.

Ventilation, grease management and acoustic separation are planned at shell stage. Retrofitting them later costs far more. See our restaurant interior design service for full scope.

data.heading: Lighting and atmosphere
data.body:
Lighting sets the mood of a restaurant more than any other element. Use warm, dimmable light in dining areas, focused light on tables, and brighter, even light at the bar, pass and kitchen.

Plan lighting scenes for different times of day: brighter for lunch service, softer and warmer for dinner.

data.heading: Acoustics and comfort
data.body: A lively room is good; a loud one sends guests home early. Hard floors, glass and bare walls reflect noise. Balance them with upholstered seating, acoustic ceiling panels, curtains and soft wall finishes.

items.question: How many seats fit per square foot?
items.answer: Roughly 15 to 20 square feet per seat including circulation. Fine dining needs more; fast casual can run tighter.

items.question: How do you control restaurant noise?
items.answer: Soft furnishings, acoustic ceiling treatment and spacing tables properly. Hard surfaces everywhere make conversation impossible at full house.

items.answer: Warm and dimmable over tables, brighter at the pass and service stations. Guests should see their food; staff should see their work.

items.question: How close should the kitchen be?

Most customers turn one way and loop the perimeter. Plan the path deliberately so every category gets seen without forcing a maze.

Trial rooms, seating and the checkout are where decisions happen. Give them light, mirrors and space, and keep them easy to reach from the main path.

data.heading: Ventilation and moisture

Lahore summers are humid during the monsoon, and small bathrooms suffer most. Without good ventilation, paint peels, grout darkens and mould appears within months.

Fit an exhaust fan that vents to the outside, not into the false ceiling. Use moisture-resistant paint on any painted surface, and keep timber finishes away from the shower zone. See our bathroom design service.

Light colours and large-format tiles make small bathrooms feel bigger because there are fewer grout lines to break up the surface. Running the same tile from floor to wall makes the room read as one continuous space.

Add a warm light over the mirror and a softer ceiling light. A frameless glass screen instead of a curtain keeps sightlines open and makes the room feel larger.

data.heading: Sightlines and light
data.body:
Small rooms feel bigger when you can see through them. Keep the line from the door to the window clear, and avoid tall pieces that cut the room in half.

Light multiplies the effect. Pale surfaces bounce daylight deeper, and layered lighting keeps corners from going dead at night.

data.heading: Multipurpose zones
data.body:
In compact homes each zone should do two jobs. A dining table that doubles as a work desk. A guest room with a daybed and proper storage.

The trick is defining zones without walls: rugs, lighting and joinery edges can mark boundaries while the space stays open.

data.body:
Light, warm neutrals make walls recede and reflect daylight. Use one main colour across connected rooms and add contrast through wood, fabrics and art rather than strong paint on every wall.

Matt and satin finishes avoid glare. Repeating the same wood tone in joinery and furniture makes a small home feel calm and planned, rather than filled.

items.question: What is the smallest practical kitchen layout?
items.answer: A single-wall or L layout of about 8 to 10 feet works well with full-height storage on one side. Keep the sink, hob and fridge in a tight triangle.

items.question: Do mirrors actually help small rooms?
items.answer: Placed opposite a window, a large mirror doubles the sense of light and depth. Small scattered mirrors just add clutter.

items.question: Is custom joinery worth it in a small flat?
items.answer: Usually yes. Standard furniture wastes the awkward corners and heights where compact homes lose the most space.

items.question: Can a small home still feel premium?
items.answer: Premium comes from proportion, light and finish quality, not square footage. Tight, well detailed rooms photograph and live better than loose large ones.

pages.title: Privacy Policy
pages.excerpt: This page explains what information Woodex Interior collects through this website, why we collect it, and the choices you have. It applies to our contact forms, cost estimator, live chat and WhatsApp enquiries.

seo.title: Privacy Policy | Woodex Interior
seo.description: How Woodex Interior collects, uses and protects your information when you contact us, use the cost estimator or chat with our team.

data.heading: Privacy policy
data.text: This page explains what information Woodex Interior collects through this website, why we collect it, and the choices you have. It applies to our contact forms, cost estimator, live chat and WhatsApp enquiries.

data.heading: 1. Information you give us
data.body: When you send an enquiry, use the cost estimator, start a live chat or message us on WhatsApp, you may share your name, phone number, email address, project type, approximate area and anything you write in the message. The estimator also stores the service, size and finish level you select so our team can follow up with a realistic range.

data.heading: 2. Information collected automatically
data.body: We record which pages are viewed on this website (the page path only) to understand which services people are interested in. This counter does not use cookies and does not identify you. The site does not run third-party advertising or remarketing pixels.

data.heading: 3. Cookies and local storage
data.body: We do not use advertising cookies. The site may store a small preference in your browser (local storage) for the chat widget so it remembers your conversation during a visit. You can clear this at any time through your browser settings.

facts.value: To reply to your enquiry and prepare a quotation or site visit.
To deliver the estimate you requested and improve our pricing ranges.
To operate the live chat and continue the conversation on WhatsApp if you choose to.
To keep basic business records (quotations, invoices, project correspondence).

data.heading: 5. Who stores your data
data.body: Form and chat data is stored in our database, hosted by Supabase, and the website itself is served by Vercel. When you click a WhatsApp button, you leave our site and message through WhatsApp (Meta) under its own privacy policy. We never sell your information, and we do not share it with advertisers.

data.heading: 6. How long we keep it
data.body: Enquiries, quotations and invoices are kept for as long as needed for your project and for legal record-keeping in Pakistan. Old chat transcripts and inactive leads are reviewed periodically and deleted or anonymised when no longer useful.

data.heading: 7. Your choices and rights
data.text: You can ask us what data we hold about you, request a correction, or ask us to delete it, by emailing info@woodex.com.pk from the address you used, or by calling the studio. We respond within a reasonable time and in any case within 30 days.

data.heading: 8. Security
data.body: Website administration is protected by role-based accounts and signed sessions. Data in transit is encrypted with HTTPS. Access to the database is limited to our application servers only.

data.heading: 9. Changes to this policy
data.body:
If we change how the website handles data, we will update this page and revise the effective date above. Continued use of the site after an update means you accept the revised policy.

data.heading: The brief
data.body:
A corner unit with good morning footfall and a long, dead afternoon. The counter jams at peak hour and the seats feel leftover.

We split the crowd by habit. Quick coffee near the counter, long stays at the back, and lighting that shifts from morning bright to evening warm.

facts.value: Counter flow in one line. Order, pay and collect run in a single line. Staff never cross the queue and peak hour stops jamming.
A seating mix, not rows. Counter stools for quick coffee, two-tops for laptops, a long table for groups. Every visit finds its seat.
Lighting that shifts. Bright and cool at breakfast, warm and low by evening. The café changes mood without changing a bulb.
Surfaces for service. Solid counters, sealed timber and washable walls stand up to spills, mopping and years of daily use.

data.heading: Takeaways
data.body:
Counter flow is throughput. Get it right and queues vanish.

Mixed seating serves more visit types than more seats.

Lighting can run two cafés in one room.

data.heading: The brief
data.body:
A compact apartment with one bedroom and a long living space. The owner works from home and hosts family most weekends.

Instead of splitting the plan into smaller rooms, we keep it open and give everything a home. Storage becomes architecture, and sightlines make it feel twice the size.

facts.value: The storage wall. A full-height wall of joinery runs one side of the flat. It holds the kitchen, wardrobe, desk and laundry in one line.
Sightlines that lie. Clear views from entry to window make the flat feel open. Furniture stays low so light travels the full length.
One room, three jobs. Living, work and dining share one space with a table that extends and lighting that changes the mood.
Bedroom with a borrowed view. A glazed screen, not a wall, separates the bedroom. Daylight reaches the corridor and privacy stays intact.

data.heading: Takeaways
data.body:
Storage is the plan in a small home. Solve it first.

Open plans need zones, not just fewer walls.

Lighting does more for size than paint colour.

items.question: What is renovation?
items.answer: Renovation upgrades an existing space through layout changes, improved services, new finishes, joinery or furniture.

items.question: How is renovation different from fit-out?
items.answer: Renovation improves an existing interior. Fit-out completes a shell or unfinished space for first use.

items.question: Can work happen while the space is occupied?
items.answer: Often, yes. Work can be phased room by room, floor by floor or outside normal operating hours.

items.question: Do you provide a condition survey?
items.answer: Yes. The survey identifies what must be replaced and what can be retained or repaired.

items.question: Is 3D design included?
items.answer: It is included when the renovation needs a new design direction. Smaller refreshes may not require it.

items.question: How is the budget controlled?
items.answer: An itemized BOQ sets out every trade, room and material before the renovation programme begins.

items.question: How long does a renovation take?
items.answer: A focused refresh can take 1 to 3 weeks. A full home, floor or multi-zone project can take 4 to 10 weeks.

data.body: Sialkot's export industry sets the standard here: offices, showrooms and owner homes with real pride in the detail. Clients often know exactly what they want visitors to see. We run these projects from Lahore with scheduled visits and clear milestones.

items.question: Do you work outside Lahore?
items.answer: Yes. Our studio is in Lahore and we take projects across Pakistan, including Sialkot. Design, drawings and coordination run from Lahore, with site visits scheduled through each phase.

items.question: How do site visits work?
items.answer: We plan visits around milestones: first measurement, mid-work checks and finishing. You always know the date before we travel.

items.question: Can you start from drawings only?
items.answer: Yes. If you have architectural drawings, we develop the design and quantities from them and verify everything on our first site visit.

items.question: Can you design a showroom for export buyers?
items.answer: Yes. We design Sialkot showrooms and offices to receive international visitors, with detailing that shows the business well.
